newsitem.title: USA: U.S. COTTON CROP SEEN AT 17.47 TO 18.15 MLN BALES.
newsitem.headline: U.S. COTTON CROP SEEN AT 17.47 TO 18.15 MLN BALES.

text.p: Prospects of good yields in Texas and poor yields in the Delta region were expected to put the U.S. Department of Agriculture's forecast for the 1997/98 cotton crop near 18 million bales, cotton analysts said.
Analysts and traders estimated this year's harvest at between 17.47 million and 18.15 million (480-lb) bales, with most estimates clustered near the high side of the range.
On July 11, USDA estimated this year's cotton crop at 18.00 million bales, down from 18.94 million bales produced in 1996/97 (Aug/July).

USDA's report, due at 0730 CDT/1230 GMT on August 12, is significant as it represents the first attempt of the season by USDA to measure crop potential by onsight surveys of yields and harvested acreage, analysts said.
"This is the first month that the USDA estimates a yield and harvested acreage," said National Cotton Council agricultural economist Kevin Brinkley.
He noted that this season, parts of Texas had excellent subsoil moisture and seasonal rains during planting.
But in the Delta, Brinkley said springtime rains slowed the planting process and delayed crop development.
John Bondurant, president of Bondurant Futures, forecasted the crop at 18.15 million bales, citing expected high yields in Texas and low yields in the Delta.

Carl Anderson, cotton specialist with Texas A and M University said, "on the plus side, we are seeing better yields in California, Arizona and some west Texas cotton areas. He projected cotton production at 18 million bales.
But he stressed it was still early in the season and even though the crop is showing stress mainly in Alabama, Missouri, Arkansas and Louisiana, it was still looking like an average cotton crop.
Smith Barney senior vice president David Brandon said he expected 17.97 million bales and Dunavant Enterprises projected the crop at 17.9 million bales.

Clustered in a group were Prudential Securities vice president Ernest Simon with an assessment of 17.75 million bales, Jernigan Group with 17.6 million bales and Calcot Ltd cotton analyst Jarral Neeper with 17.5 million bales.
"I expect USDA to indicate a potential U.S. crop of 18 million bales or higher but when it is all said, I think the final crop will come in around 17.5 million," Neeper said.
On the low end was Sharon Johnson, cotton analyst with Frank Schneider and Co, projecting 17.47 million bales.
"That is a drop of 530,000 bales below the July USDA estimate and we're using a 631-lb per acre yield and abandonment just under five percent," she said.

The Delta should see a fairly substantial production decrease due to less planted acreage and lower expected yields and the southwest, including Texas and Oklahoma, should be substantially above last year due to greater acreage, Johnson said.
